analysis.one_liner: Restores gun-violence victims' right to sue firearm makers and sellers.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Judiciary Committee without a hearing, a vote, or any action after its 2017 referral.
analysis.plain_summary: A 2005 federal law, the Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act, blocks most lawsuits against gun and ammunition makers, sellers, dealers, and their trade association when their products are used to hurt people. This bill would repeal that shield, letting victims of gun violence take manufacturers and sellers to court under ordinary product-liability and negligence rules, the same as nearly every other industry.
analysis.who_benefits: People injured by gun violence and families of those killed, who would regain the ability to sue manufacturers, sellers, importers, dealers, and trade associations over how a gun was made, marketed, or sold into unlawful hands. Courts and state attorneys general would also regain tools, since lawsuits are how the public learns what the industry knew and did.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals sections 2, 3, and 4 of the Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act, which prohibit civil actions against firearm or ammunition manufacturers, sellers, importers, dealers, and trade associations for the criminal or unlawful misuse of a firearm [S2] [S3].

Restoring those civil claims would put gun companies under the same liability rules as other consumer-product makers, giving victims a path to compensation and a discovery process that can expose negligent sales and marketing practices [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Firearm and ammunition manufacturers, sellers, dealers, importers, and the industry trade association, which would face civil lawsuits they are currently shielded from, including defense costs, judgments, and higher liability insurance. Some of those costs would likely be passed into gun prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gun makers, sellers, and their trade association

drawbacks.text: The 2005 law exists because Congress concluded that sellers should not be held liable when a criminal misuses a lawful product they sold; repealing it would expose dealers and manufacturers to litigation over third-party crimes they did not commit, which supporters of the shield argue could pressure lawful businesses and raise gun prices for buyers [S2].

Civil suits are slow, costly, and uncertain; victims could spend years in court against well-funded industry defendants even after the shield was lifted, and a repeal alone would not guarantee compensation in any individual case [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to victims is significant and concrete: it removes the only blanket liability shield of its kind and lets courts decide negligence claims case by case, the way other industries are handled. The cost falls on gun companies and would partly show up in prices, and opponents' warning about liability for third-party crimes is a genuine policy dispute — but it is the same dispute every other product industry resolves through ordinary liability law. On balance the bill's main effect would be to shift decision-making about gun safety from Congress's 2005 blanket protection back to courts and juries.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee in October 2017 and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Blumenthal introduced the bill on October 5, 2017, joined by 18 Democratic cosponsors and one Independent [S1] [S3] [S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day [S5].
The action history shows no further action — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote — before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Firearm and ammunition manufacturers, sellers, dealers, and the industry trade association are better off, because the liability shield protecting them from most gun-violence lawsuits remains in force. Victims of gun violence remain unable to bring the civil actions this bill would have restored.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gun industry keeps its lawsuit shield

for.name: Sen. Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the gun industry's liability shield.

for.name: Sen. Chris Murphy and 17 other Democrats and one Independent
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Murphy (D-CT), Markey (D-MA), Menendez (D-NJ), Sanders (I-VT), Gillibrand (D-NY), Warren (D-MA), and Booker (D-NJ).

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on October 5, 2017 and took no action on it — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor; the bill stayed in committee through the end of the 115th Congress.

against.name: Firearm industry and gun-rights groups
against.role: Opponents of repealing the Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act
against.what_they_did: Defended the 2005 liability shield that the bill sought to repeal; the shield remained law.

sides.party_line_note: All 20 supporters were Democrats plus one Independent; no Republican cosponsored, and the bill died in committee with no recorded votes on either side.

industries.note: The bill would have removed the industry's unique protection from civil suits when its products are criminally or unlawfully misused, exposing it to negligence and product-liability claims [S2] [S3]. Because the bill died, the industry keeps that shield; its protection from lawsuits comes at the cost of victims' access to court.

industries.industry: Firearm dealers, sellers, importers, and trade associations
industries.note: The 2005 law shields dealers and even the industry trade association from suits over unlawful misuse of guns they sold or promoted; repeal would have made them answerable in court like other sellers of consumer products [S2] [S3].

industries.industry: Liability insurers for the gun industry
industries.note: Repeal would have created a wave of new litigation exposure for gun-industry clients, raising defense and insurance costs — but only if the bill had advanced, which it did not [S3].
